comments.author: igorandri

Igor here, Head of Security at Lovable. Thanks to the Crissy Field team for their work.
The root cause in these apps was insufficent Row-Level Security, which is exactly what our scanning is built to catch. We scan every app automatically before publish and offer a deeper SAST scan, both free for all users. When we flag findings, users can select “Fix” and Lovable will help resolve them. They can also enable auto-fix, which resolves security findings in the background, and block publishing entirely when there are critical findings.
When an app has end users, security is a key part of the product. That’s why we keep investing in making security tools better and easier to use, taking on as much of the security load as we can and fixing more issues automatically.
I personally believe that making security accessible is what leads to making software accessible. We’re committed to both.
You can read more about our approach:
https://lovable.dev/blog/find-it-fix-it-ship-it

stories.title_en: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer?

comments.author: femto
comments.text:
What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists).  You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ.  Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it.  8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart.  There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory.
Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"?  It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.

comments.author: kamma4434
comments.text:
For what it’s worth: when I used to do assembly on the commodore 64, after a while, your eyes are so used to seeing A9 close to LDA let you start knowing them by heart without even thinking. Of course this is possible on 6502 and will be way harder on modern CPUs. In the end of the number of common opcodes might have been 30-50, and you can always look up the rest from a one-page table.
I remember that was a book that went on to say that you should learn machine code (that is, raw opcodes), not assembly, to program the c-64. Not sure I would agree, but it’s definitely feasible.
The only thing that is strange in the Woz story is that you would usually start by creating a dirt-poor monitor/assembler so that you would have a sane environment to do further development in. That was the approach manuals from the era suggested for new hardware (eg Rodnay Zack’s)

comments.author: runjake
comments.text:
I don’t know about other people, but back in the early 80s, I spent a lot of time writing code (mostly assembler, some BASIC and other dead languages) with pencil on paper for various reasons: sometimes I preferred it, sometimes I was writing code for computers I only had access to in labs or at school.
There were even pre-made paper forms for writing code, like the IBM COBOL program sheets and similar for assembler.
Even now, if I’m working on a tough issue, I still print out code sections on paper and hash it out with a pencil.

comments.author: II2II
comments.text:
Follow-up question: how did Woz get BASIC into ROM?
The handwritten interpreter is fairly common knowledge since Woz has told that story many times, but I don't recall any accounts of how he bridged the gap from paper to silicon. All of the discussion about the machine language monitor doesn't really address the question. At best, it moves the question from programming a ROM for BASIC to programming a ROM with the machine language monitor. Even with the monitor, additional hardware would be required to program a ROM. At the very least, a latch would be required to hold the address and data. Of course, it is possible that he did it without the computer (using a rig that let him "toggle" the pins). It is also possible that he used another computer to program the ROM, but, as he said, he didn't have the money to program BASIC on a computer so why would that be different for a ROM?

comments.author: mrandish
comments.text:
I got my first computer in 1981, a 4K Radio Shack Color Computer for $500 (a huge purchase decision at the time). So I missed hand assembling for bare metal and Altair-type toggles.
However, there was an interesting period of a few years where assembler tools were either unavailable or fairly expensive, so it was common to use the computer's BASIC to write an assembly language monitor program. Such program listings were pretty common in early hobbyist 'zines. It was also pretty common to use BASIC to POKE in a quick bootstrap program to load a value in a register and jump to an address, which I could usually do from memory. After 40 years I still remember the 6809 RTS was $39 and NOP was $12, two very handy instructions to POKE a quick mod into a program.

comments.author: codeflo
comments.text: The community-driven quest for "panic safety" in Rust is the same curse that befell C++ in terms of "exception safety", maybe worse because at least more C++ shops are sensible enough to disable exceptions. It's simply not practical to think through 20 convoluted edge cases for every innocent little function, which means that no realistic program will safely recover from a panic. It's best to admit this and engineer your system accordingly.

comments.author: jonathanlydall

In addition to regular unit tests, we use Playwright to test our Electron app and also allow agents to drive our app using Playwright via MCP to validate their work or investigate bugs.
Based on past experience of the extreme fragility of testing against the DOM, I had Claude build an "automation API" for generally interacting with our app. Instead of LLMs needing to have Playwright click buttons or manually fill in forms or things like that, it instead executes scripts against a well defined API which we have our Angular "controllers" attach themselves to on "load" and then detach from on "unload".
So LLMs use pure JavaScript via the API and don't really need to use the DOM to interact with the app, but will do snapshots of the DOM as needed when investigating any bugs or visual issues.

very

Citrus ancestry is stupidly complex, and the generally commercially available varieties sadly few.
You may have heard of yuzu, which was a foodie fad a couple of years ago (and deservedly so, it smells & tastes great). In Japan, it's only one of numerous citruses, including dekopon (navel mandarins, occasional sold in Australia as "sumo"), tachibana, kabosu, sudachi, etc.
Hop a few islands down to Okinawa, and the fruits change yet again! Here you have shikwasa (hirami lemon), tachibana, tanibuta, etc.
